lesson_title: Nine Chemicals You Already Own: Common Acids and Bases
hook_text: Your Grade 11 chemistry syllabus is hiding in your kitchen, your bathroom and your garage.
clip_script: Nine chemicals carry the whole acid-base section of your chemistry paper — and you own most of them already. Kitchen: the vinegar is ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, mild enough to eat because it's weak and lazy about giving up its hydrogen. The baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate — the fizz in your vetkoek. Laundry: washing soda, sodium carbonate, baking soda's tougher sibling with two sodiums. Under the sink: caustic soda, sodium hydroxide, the base that eats hair clogs. That sharp-smelling window cleaner? Ammonia — a base with no hydroxide in its formula at all, chemistry's great trick question. Now the garage: pool acid is hydrochloric acid, the exact same acid your stomach brews every day. And the car battery runs on sulphuric acid, carrying TWO acidic hydrogens where the others carry one. Here's the secret the exam is really testing: you don't memorise these formulae. You build them — charges snap together until they hit zero, like magnets. Nine chemicals. One house. Free marks.
visual_style: A fast room-to-room house tour with each bottle freezing mid-frame while its chemical formula stamps over the label; end on ions clicking together like magnetic tiles totalling zero.
mood: Familiar and revelatory — the syllabus discovered on the viewer's own shelves.
pacing: Rapid room-hopping beats, a slow-down on the ammonia trick, snap-together finale.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn your house into your formula sheet.
